blurb: TPUs, hyperscalers' custom silicon, inference startups and the AI chips in your phone and laptop.

cards.title: A chip built for one job

steps.p: Around 2013, Google projected that if users spoke to voice search a few minutes a day, it would need to double its data centers.
The TPU's core is a grid of multiply-accumulate units. Data flows through it in waves, each unit passing results to its neighbor.
Later TPUs connect thousands of chips with dedicated links into pods that train one model together.

cards.aside: The first TPU went into Google's data centers in 2015 and was announced publicly in 2016.

cards.q: Why is a systolic array efficient for matrix multiplication?
options: It uses less silicon than a CPU
Data is reused as it flows between neighboring units, avoiding repeated trips to memory
It runs at higher clock speeds
cards.why: Data reuse. Each number read from memory is used by many units as it passes through, so arithmetic far outpaces memory access.

cards.statement: The first-generation TPU was designed only for inference, not training.
cards.why: True. TPU v1 ran 8-bit integer math to serve models. Training support arrived with TPU v2 in 2017.

cards.title: Google's Ironwood TPU, announced in 2025, was its first designed specifically for inference at scale — and comes in pods of 9,216 chips.
cards.detail: Google positioned it for the "age of inference", as serving models to users, especially reasoning models, overtakes training as the main compute demand.

cards.statement: You can buy Google's data-center TPUs to install in your own servers.
cards.why: False. They are available through Google Cloud, not sold as standalone parts. (Google's small Edge TPU for embedded devices is a separate product.)

cards.q: What drove Google to start the TPU project?
options: Projections that neural network workloads like speech recognition would otherwise require doubling its data centers
cards.why: Cost of scale. A custom chip far more efficient for neural networks was cheaper than building many more data centers of general-purpose hardware.

cards.title: Everyone builds their own

steps.p: Amazon (Trainium, Inferentia), Microsoft (Maia) and Meta (MTIA) design their own AI accelerators.
Lower cost per workload, less dependence on NVIDIA's supply and pricing, and chips tuned to their own models.
Software ecosystems take years to mature, and NVIDIA's CUDA lead is hard to match.

cards.aside: Most of these chips are made by TSMC — the same foundry NVIDIA uses.

cards.q: Amazon's custom chip for training AI models is called…
cards.why: Trainium. Graviton is Amazon's general-purpose CPU, Maia is Microsoft's AI chip, and Ironwood is Google's TPU.

cards.statement: Anthropic uses Amazon's Trainium chips to train models.
cards.why: True. Amazon's Project Rainier built a large Trainium cluster for Anthropic, which also uses Google TPUs and NVIDIA GPUs.

cards.title: Cerebras builds a single chip the size of an entire silicon wafer.
cards.detail: Its Wafer Scale Engine 3 covers about 46,000 mm² with around 4 trillion transistors — roughly 50 times the area of a large GPU — keeping huge amounts of memory on-chip.

cards.statement: AMD's MI300X GPU carries more high-bandwidth memory than NVIDIA's H100.
cards.why: True. 192 GB versus 80 GB. More memory per chip lets large models fit on fewer GPUs — a key selling point for inference.

cards.q: What is the biggest obstacle for NVIDIA's competitors?
options: The maturity and familiarity of NVIDIA's software ecosystem
cards.why: Software. Matching raw hardware performance is feasible; getting every framework, library and developer workflow to run smoothly takes years.

cards.title: Specialize to go faster

steps.p: GPUs handle training, inference, graphics and science — flexible but not optimal for any single task.
Startups like Groq and Cerebras design chips that generate tokens extremely fast, often by keeping weights in on-chip memory.
Specialized chips win if workloads stay stable. If model architectures change, they risk obsolescence.

cards.aside: Flexibility versus efficiency is the oldest trade-off in chip design.

cards.q: Groq's inference chips get their speed largely by keeping model weights in…
options: On-chip SRAM spread across many chips
cards.why: SRAM. On-chip SRAM is far faster than off-chip HBM but holds much less, so a large model must be split across many chips.

cards.statement: A chip designed only to run transformers would struggle if the dominant AI architecture changed.
cards.why: True. That is the risk of extreme specialization. Hard-wiring today's design gives big efficiency gains but little room to adapt.

cards.q: Compared with a GPU, a custom ASIC for a fixed task is usually…
options: Slower and more expensive to run
cards.why: Efficiency for flexibility. Dropping hardware for unneeded tasks saves power and area, but the chip can do less.

cards.title: Groq was founded by Jonathan Ross, who worked on the original Google TPU.
cards.detail: Many AI chip startups trace back to the TPU team, which proved that custom silicon for neural networks could beat general-purpose hardware.

cards.q: Why don't all chips just use SRAM instead of HBM?
options: SRAM is far less dense and more expensive per byte
SRAM uses more power when idle only
cards.why: Density and cost. SRAM needs about six transistors per bit and lives on the expensive logic die. HBM stores far more per dollar.

cards.title: Neural processing units

steps.p: Phones and laptops now include NPUs — small accelerators for neural network math — beside the CPU and GPU.
On-device AI is private, works offline, responds instantly, and costs nothing per use.
NPU speed is quoted in trillions of operations per second, usually at low precision.

cards.aside: Face unlock, photo processing, live captions and dictation often run on the NPU.

cards.q: Microsoft's Copilot+ PC label requires an NPU of at least how much performance?
cards.why: 40 TOPS. Microsoft set that bar in 2024 for features like Recall and live captions to run locally.

cards.statement: Apple's Neural Engine first appeared in the A11 Bionic chip in the iPhone X in 2017.
cards.why: True. It powered Face ID and Animoji. Apple's chips have included a Neural Engine ever since, growing much faster each generation.
Trillions of operations per second, usually measured with 8-bit integers. Comparisons across vendors are rough, as precision and real-world utilization differ.

cards.title: Face ID matches your face entirely on the iPhone, never sending it to Apple's servers.
cards.detail: The Neural Engine compares a depth map of your face with a stored mathematical representation, all on-device — a privacy benefit of local AI.

cards.title: Find your laptop's NPU
cards.body: On Windows 11, Task Manager's Performance tab lists an NPU if your laptop has a supported one, showing when it is in use.
cards.challenge: Open Task Manager (Ctrl+Shift+Esc) → Performance, and check whether an NPU appears.
